newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina gets 1st investment-grade credit ratings.
newsitem.headline: Argentina gets 1st investment-grade credit ratings.

text.p: Argentina got its first investment-grade credit ratings this week in a move hailed as another boost to its improving financial credentials.

"This is major news at the corporate level," said Esteban Thomsen, Argentina economist at ING Barings, referring to a new corporate risk policy announced by Standard & Poor's late Tuesday that removes the sovereign ratings ceiling on Argentine corporations.

S&P said it concluded the high level of dollarization in Argentina's economy meant the ability of corporations to pay foreign debts will not be impeded by the government, "even in a scenario involving sovereign default."
Dollarization is a process whereby the dollar or another hard currency replaces the local currency as the main store of value in a country with a history of high inflation.
Effectively, S&P said that, only in very extreme cases will the government be able to prevent companies from transferring foreign currency out of the country, analysts said.
"Everybody will benefit from this," said Frank McGann, first vice-president at Merrill Lynch Argentina. "It underpins my positive outlook for the long-term."
But most of all, the financial institutions and corporate issuers that were upgraded, in most cases by as much as two grades, stand to gain.
Dolores Lopez Larroy, head of research at Deutsche Bank Argentina, estimated yields on the foreign bonds of those issuers could fall around 100 basis points.
"Most of all new bond issues will see lower spreads," she said.
Argentina's sovereign foreign currency rating is BB.
In addition, Camuzzi Gas Pampeana, Camuzzi Gas del Sur and Metrogas SA were placed on "credit watch with positive outlook."
Larroy said the news could lead the companies with better ratings to take advantage of anticipated improved conditions by redeeming old debt and issuing new.
"This will also have an impact on equity because financing for the companies will be cheaper," said ING Barings' Thomsen.
That impact may not be immediate, as the lower financing will not feed through to corporates profits for some time.
Even so, Banco Frances was among top stock performers Tuesday, rising 4.1 percent on the Buenos Aires Stock Exchange.
Metrogas was the main winner mid-session on Wednesday, posting a rise of 5.1 percent.

Besides these upgrades opening up the doors for a new pool of investors for the firms' bonds, stocks could get a boost because there are some specific funds that are also not allowed to invest in stocks of companies that are speculative- grade.
Despite being seen as positive news for Argentina's economy as a whole, Larroy cautioned that "this in no way means Argentina will be investment grade at the end of the year, as some people think."
Indeed, S&P said the move was unrelated to its recent upgrade of Argentina's sovereign credit rating to BB from BB-.
